Today, as she slid into a seat near the back, she was leaning toward ironic. She'd drunk three cups this morning. She wasn't prepared to feel guilty about it.

"The price you pay at the café," Mr. Chen began, tapping the board, "almost never reflects what the farmer actually receives." He sketched a supply chain: farmer at the left, then middleman, then exporter, then roaster, then café, then consumer. Each layer got smaller—a visual representation of how the money distributed itself as it moved right. Alexandra watched the other students lean forward. She recognized the gesture: they were about to learn something that would make them feel morally complicated. "A farmer in Ethiopia might receive fifteen cents for beans that sell for five dollars," he said. "Why? Because the farmer has no leverage. No way to reach the buyer directly. No choice but to sell to the middleman, who sets the price."

The discussion that followed split almost immediately. Jasmine, who always had her hand up first, argued that the solution was fair-trade certification. "If we just knew which coffee was ethically sourced, we'd buy it. Consumer power." Alexandra found herself nodding. It made sense: choice, information, individual action. Clean. The opposite of the basement they were sitting in. But then Marcus, who rarely spoke and seemed to be genuinely thinking rather than performing thought, said something quieter. "Fair-trade coffee costs more. So mostly richer people buy it. The farmers selling regular coffee are still stuck getting fifteen cents."

Mr. Chen didn't interrupt. He let the silence sit there, which Alexandra had learned was his favorite teaching move. It was also his most annoying one. After a moment, he asked, "What would leverage actually look like for a farmer?" and the room got uncertain. Someone suggested cooperatives. Someone else said governments should regulate prices. Jasmine countered that that would reduce demand. Alexandra found herself thinking about the diagram on the board—not the chain itself, but the gaps between each link. Those gaps were where the leverage lived, or didn't.

She raised her hand, something she almost never did in this class. "But how would you know if you fixed it?" Mr. Chen's eyebrows went up. He looked genuinely interested, which was somehow worse than looking encouraging. "Like, if farmers had more leverage and got more money, would coffee stay the same price or go up? And how would you tell if the system actually changed or if someone just moved where they were taking their cut?"

The seminar ended before he could answer, which felt deliberate on the universe's part. During lunch, Alexandra found herself thinking about disparate parts of the problem that seemed to pull in different directions. If farmers earned more, either consumers paid more or the café owner made less. But raising the price would mean fewer people bought coffee, which meant less demand, which meant farmers might earn even less from selling more volume at lower prices. Or the middleman might just take the extra. There was no obvious point of leverage that didn't create a new problem somewhere else.

Two days later, in the same seminar, Mr. Chen handed out a spreadsheet. It was a real supply chain from a real coffee company—the prices paid at each stage, the quantities involved, the profit margins. "I want you to identify where change could actually happen," he said. "Not where it should happen. Where someone with power could make it happen and why they might or might not." Alexandra worked through it with Jasmine and Marcus, and this time something clicked. The exporter made a thirty percent margin. The roaster made twenty-five percent. The farmer made three percent. But the farmer sold far more volume than anyone else—they were just paid so little per unit that it didn't matter. The café, meanwhile, barely moved product at scale. Its power wasn't in volume. It was in reputation.

"If enough cafés refused to buy from exporters who didn't pay a certain price, it might actually matter," Marcus said, pointing at the numbers. "But only if they coordinated. And only if they could afford to turn away supply." Jasmine was already shaking her head. "That's price-fixing. That's illegal." "Only if competitors agree," Alexandra said. "But if they all do it separately—just decide their ethics matter—is that illegal?" Nobody knew. She paid for the coffee, pulled out her phone, and searched for the farmer's name to see what else she could find.

Lily sat on the floor of her childhood playroom, surrounded by colored paper, scissors, and glue that had gone slightly tacky in its bottle. The room had been undisturbed for two years, since she'd left for her gap year, and it still held the particular quiet of a space waiting to be remembered. She was making a collage for her college dorm, she'd told her mother, though what she was actually doing felt less purposeful than that. She was arranging and rearranging images cut from magazines—a photograph of hands holding soil, a word fragment that read "solvency," a painting of a horse in profile—trying to make something that would mean what she couldn't yet say.

Her younger sister Maya appeared in the doorway, still in her soccer uniform. "You're being so weird about this," Maya said, not unkindly. She sat down beside Lily and picked up a piece of the collage that Lily had discarded. It showed a person's face half-obscured by shadow. "Why are you cutting them apart? Why not just, like, take a photo of something you like?"

"Because a photo is just what's there," Lily said. She held up her work, the collection of disparate images still not quite forming into anything coherent. "When you cut things up and put them next to each other, they make new meanings. Things that wouldn't normally talk to each other suddenly do."

Maya considered this, turning the discarded image in her hands. "That's just random, though. You're just putting things together and hoping it makes sense."

The conversation stayed with Lily as Maya left to shower. She returned to her collage, but something in the exchange had unsettled her. Was she making meaning or manufacturing it? The difference seemed important but difficult to locate. She'd always believed that if you combined symbols—words, images, colors—deliberately enough, something true would emerge. But Maya's skepticism had introduced a crack in that certainty. What if the meaning she felt she was discovering was only the meaning she'd already decided to project? What if there was no actual communication happening at all, only the performance of it?

She began an experiment. She selected images and words deliberately and pasted them without intention, letting chance guide her. A photograph of an empty field. The word "wait." A fragment showing a person's hand reaching toward something out of frame. She worked in this mode for nearly an hour, her mind becoming quiescent, her hands moving in a steady rhythm that required no decision. When she stepped back, something had shifted. The collage didn't feel random anymore. It felt haunting in a way that surprised her. But how? She'd removed choice from the process, yet the meaning seemed even more enthrall­ing, more present than when she'd labored over every decision.

She understood then what had happened. The meaning wasn't created by her intention or by chance alone. It was created in the act of looking. She had made choices about what to keep, what sequence to place things in, what space to leave between them. But those choices had been intuitive rather than conscious. The collision of images had suggested something neither image contained alone—not because she'd projected meaning onto them, but because meaning existed in the gap between symbols. Language worked this way too, she realized. A word meant nothing by itself; it meant something in relation to other words, in context, in the space between speaker and listener.

She picked up a pencil and drew a line across the collage from the empty field to the reaching hand. It was a small gesture, but it changed how the whole thing moved. Someone looking at it would complete the motion with their own eye, their own imagination. They would bring their own meanings into the space she'd created. It wouldn't be her meaning they saw exactly. It would be theirs, or something that lived between them.

Lily photographed the collage with her phone and sent it to Maya without explanation. While she waited for a response, she began gathering the scraps of paper that covered the floor, preserving only a few pieces she might use again.

Cohen's fingers hovered over the keyboard in the fluorescent silence of the community center's basement computer lab. The screen in front of him displayed a simple Python script, twenty lines of code that should have printed out the numbers one through ten. Instead, it had printed nothing at all.

"You're missing a colon," said Priya from the next terminal over, not looking up from her own work. She had been coming to these Saturday afternoon coding sessions for three months; Cohen had started two weeks ago.

He found it: line seven, after the for loop. One small mark he'd omitted, and the whole thing collapsed. As he typed it in, the numbers appeared on screen, and something in his chest unclenched. The mesmerize quality of watching a machine do exactly what you told it to do hadn't worn off yet. He wondered if it ever would.

"Why does it have to be so exact?" he asked. "Like, why can't the computer just figure out what I meant?"

Priya leaned back in her chair, considering. "Because a computer isn't a person. It can't guess. It can only follow rules." She paused. "My mom's a doctor. She studies immunology, and she's always saying that the immune system has these incredibly specific rules about what counts as a threat and what doesn't. If the rules get messed up, nothing works right. I think programming is kind of like that. The computer's whole job is to follow the rules exactly."

Cohen thought about that while Priya turned back to her screen. He'd come to these sessions because his guidance counselor had suggested it after his grade in history kept sliding. "You need a different way to think," Mrs. Chen had said, which felt specious, like an excuse to push him toward something he hadn't asked for. But his mom had enrolled him anyway, and he'd been surprised to find himself coming back.

Over the next hour, he worked through a simple debugging exercise. The instructor, a college student named Marcus, had provided a program that was supposed to calculate someone's age based on their birth year. It had bugs deliberately planted in it. The exercise was to find them and fix them. Cohen worked through it slowly, running the program, watching it fail, reading the error messages. He started to recognize patterns: when a variable was spelled wrong, the error said one thing. When there was a logic problem, it said something else. The computer was trying to tell him what was wrong.

He was nearly done when he realized something. The oldest bug in the program wasn't a typo at all. It was in the logic. The original code had been written in 1995, Marcus had noted in the comments, and it calculated age by subtracting the birth year from 1995. But now it was 2024. Someone had copied that code and forgotten to update the number. They'd just left it there, and the program had been giving wrong answers for decades without anyone noticing or fixing it.

Cohen stared at it, understanding something larger than the exercise. History wasn't just about what happened long ago. It was embedded in the things people made, and if you weren't paying attention, if you just assumed that old answers still worked, you'd keep getting it wrong. All those details he'd struggled to memorize in history class—the dates, the names—they mattered because without them, you didn't even know you were making a mistake.

He called Marcus over and pointed to the date bug. Marcus smiled and nodded, letting him make the fix himself. When Cohen changed 1995 to 2024, the program began calculating ages correctly.

Walking to the bus stop afterward, Priya fell into step beside him. "Same time next week?" she asked.

Cohen adjusted his backpack. "Yeah," he said. "But I think I need to go back and pay more attention in my history class too."

Priya laughed. "Those are different things."

"Are they though?" Cohen said, and neither of them answered as they waited for the light to change.

Payton sat on the bleachers with her phone in her lap, the gymnasium's fluorescent lights casting everything in a sterile white that made the basketball court look like a stage. She was supposed to be watching her younger brother Marcus play in the regional tournament, but instead she kept checking the livestream on her screen. Her club team's game was happening two hours away, and every few seconds she refreshed the feed to watch girls she trained with execute plays she knew by heart. The diaphanous veil between the two events—one she was actually present for, one happening in pixels—felt thinner than it should.

Her mother had made the trade clear: one game for the other. Payton couldn't do both. The drive to Marcus's tournament took forty-five minutes each way, and her team's match started while she'd still be in the car. When Payton had asked if she could skip Marcus's game, her mother's face had done that thing it did, a particular kind of closing off, and she'd said simply, "Your brother needs you there." So Payton was here, divided, watching a livestream of her own absence.

The thing about livestreaming your own team's game was that you could see yourself not being there. When the camera panned the bench during timeouts, you could count the bodies and know exactly who was missing. The commentator, some parent with a surprisingly decent microphone setup, mentioned it in an offhand way: "Payton Martinez usually runs that wing, but she's out this game." The camera even caught the empty spot on the bench where she would have sat, a small dark rectangle between two teammates. Payton wondered if people in the stands were noticing the gap, if they were thinking less of her team because one player wasn't there, if that single absence was enough to commodify the whole game into something worth less attention.

On court in front of her, Marcus was struggling. She could see it in the way his shoulders tensed before he caught a pass, the hesitation in his dribble. He was fourteen and still figuring out how to move his taller body through space. He'd made the regional tournament for the first time, and their mother had been quietly fervent about Payton being there. Not as a favor, exactly. As a fact. The kind of fact that didn't require explanation.

At halftime of Marcus's game, Payton's phone buzzed. A text in the team chat: they were down by eight. Down by eight at halftime in a game that mattered for seeding. Payton knew the other team's patterns. She knew what they'd adjust for the second half. She knew, with the specific knowledge that comes from being inside something, what her presence might have changed. She could feel the shape of that missing variable, the way it hung in the livestream like something almost visible.

She looked up from her phone at Marcus, who was walking toward the concession stand with the other bench players, still in his uniform, still holding the small peccadillo of the game close to himself—a missed defensive rotation that he'd probably replay in his mind for days. He hadn't asked her to come. He'd only asked once, two weeks ago, if she could make it, and when she'd explained about her tournament, he'd nodded in that way young kids do when they're trying to seem older than they are. But he'd checked the bleachers during warm-ups. She'd seen him do it.

Payton turned off the livestream. The screen went dark, and the gymnasium came back into focus with sudden clarity: the smell of hot sneakers and floor wax, the particular screech of shoes on hardwood, the sound of her mother two rows behind her eating popcorn. When Marcus came back out for the second half, his eyes found her in the stands again, and this time she waved. He lifted one hand briefly, and his shoulders seemed to relax by an inch.

During the third quarter, Marcus's team came back. It was the kind of slow, grinding comeback that doesn't feel dramatic while it's happening, just incremental work, point by point. He got two steals in a row. When he made a three-pointer late in the fourth quarter, bringing them within one, Payton found herself standing, and she realized that this—this actual, breathing, present thing—was the game she'd chosen. She would find out later, after the tournament ended, that her team had lost by six. She would see the footage of plays she might have changed. She would feel the particular sting of that absence for weeks.

But right now, in this moment, Marcus was bringing the ball down court, his face concentrated, his breath visible as small clouds in the cold gym, and Payton stayed standing, watching the one game she'd actually chosen to be present for, understanding finally that choosing to be somewhere meant accepting what you weren't choosing to be, and that there was no way to know if you'd chosen right until after it mattered.
